paras: The reported lynching of Mexican Frank was the reported killing, in late July 1882, of a man called Mexican Frank or Marion Frank by a posse near Tascosa, Oldham County, Texas, after he was accused of shooting Deputy Sheriff Henry McCullough. The news spread nationally as a brief wire item, but every version described the lynching as reported rather than confirmed. Two weeks later a Texas Ranger captain reported that the deputy's killer had been arrested, leaving the outcome in doubt.

Tascosa lay in the Texas Panhandle, where Ranger Captain Arrington described "troubles" that summer. Early telegrams garbled the town's name as "Gaseasia," "Gazasia," "Gaseala," "Gaesia" and "Guscosia" before later items gave it as Tascosa.

According to a Texas special relayed from St. Louis, "Marion Frank, a mulatto, shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Henry McCullough" in Oldham County on July 27. A dispatch datelined at the town itself put the shooting on the morning of July 28 and called the accused "a Mexican, named Frank." A "large posse" pursued him, and he was "reported caught and lynched." No report gives the place, manner or time of the killing, or names anyone in the pursuing party.

On August 11 an Austin special to the Dallas Herald said that Captain Arrington had written to the adjutant-general that "Sheriff McColloch has been killed by a gambler at Tascosa, Oldham county, who was arrested by the rangers." Arrington left five rangers at Tascosa and recommended that they be stationed there permanently. The report did not name the gambler or mention a lynching, and no account of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached papers from Dakota to California within a day as a line or two of telegraphic news. The Galveston version, printed under headlines such as "Americans Hold Their Own" in Yankton and "Reported Lynched" in Las Vegas, added that "two Mexicans were killed by a crowd of Americans" in a fight "near Fernannez." The fuller Texas special, carried by the Wheeling Register under "Two Murders and a Lynching" and by the St. Paul Globe, treated that fight as a separate killing among Mexicans near Laredo.

Later roundups dropped the word "reported": the Watertown Republican said flatly that "A mob pursued the murderer and lynched him," and a Tennessee and Mississippi item said "Frank Mulatto, a Mexican, was lynched near Tascosa." The Burlington Free Press headed its dispatch "Texas Justice." The Dallas Herald's report of an arrest ran in its daily and weekly editions; no correction appears in the papers that had carried the lynching. Papers alternately called the accused "a mulatto" and "a Mexican," and some printed "Mexican" or "Mulatto" as part of his name.

Whether Frank was killed at all is disputed: the wire reports of a lynching were all hearsay, while the Ranger captain's report to the adjutant-general said the killer was arrested. The date also varies, with July 27 in some reports and the morning of July 28 in the dispatch datelined from the town.

bases: Wire reports said a posse or mob pursued and lynched the man accused of killing a deputy sheriff (A4, A8, A12, A13), though a later state report says the killer was arrested (A18).

The only reports of a killing are wire items saying Frank was 'reported caught and lynched' by a large posse or mob for killing a deputy (A4, A6, A13), while Ranger Captain Arrington's report to the adjutant-general says the killer at Tascosa was arrested by the rangers (A18); no account confirms a death.
Several independent wire versions report a lynching, all as hearsay ('reported') (A1, A4, A13), and a Texas state report two weeks later says the killer was arrested (A18).

framing.detail: Most papers ran the item as one line among unrelated telegrams, calling Frank 'the murderer' and the lynching 'reported'.
The Dakotaian's headline 'Americans Hold Their Own' and the Burlington Free Press's 'Texas Justice' framed the news as frontier retribution, the latter possibly ironically.

versions.value: Reported caught and lynched by a posse or mob

conflicts.note: The lynching reports are all secondhand ('reported'); the Austin special relays a Ranger captain's letter written later, though its 'who was arrested' could grammatically refer to the gambler or be read loosely; it does not name the killer.
Wire copy alternately treats 'Mexican' and 'Mulatto' as part of his name or as his description.
A4's 'yesterday' is relative to a July 28 dispatch (printed 'July 23').
